name: Pioneer Lunar Program (1958-1959)
short_status: A completed, mostly failed campaign, Aug 1958 to Mar 1959: five lunar probes, four failures and one partial success. None reached the Moon; only Pioneer 4 escaped Earth's gravity, and it still circles the Sun today.

name: Luna 1
short_status: Missed its intended impact and flew past the Moon at 5,995 km on 4 Jan 1959, becoming the first spacecraft to escape Earth's gravity and orbit the Sun.

name: Luna 2
short_status: Impacted the Moon in Palus Putredinis on 13 Sep 1959 at 21:02:23 UT (00:02 on 14 Sep Moscow time): the first human-made object to reach another world.

name: Luna 3
short_status: Looped behind the Moon and photographed the far side on 7 Oct 1959; 17 of 29 film frames were received by 18 Oct, and contact was lost 22 Oct 1959.

name: Ranger Program
short_status: Nine spacecraft, 1961 to 1965: six straight failures, then Rangers 7, 8 and 9 returned the first US close-up images of the Moon before crashing into it. Program complete; last impact 24 Mar 1965 in Alphonsus crater.

name: Soviet Crewed Lunar Program
short_status: Cancelled May 1974 and kept secret until the late 1980s: the USSR's two-track effort to beat Apollo. Cosmonaut-class Zond hardware looped the Moon uncrewed, but all four launches of the N1 Moon rocket failed and no Soviet ever left Earth orbit.

name: Luna soft-landing failures (E-6, 1963 to 1965)
short_status: Failure, over and over: between January 1963 and December 1965 the Soviet E-6 program ran up eleven straight soft-landing failures, three of them crashing on the Moon (Luna 5, Luna 7, Luna 8), before Luna 9 finally landed on the twelfth attempt in February 1966.

name: Luna 10
short_status: Entered lunar orbit 3 Apr 1966, the first artificial satellite of another world; 460 orbits and 219 radio sessions before batteries died 30 May 1966; later crashed at an unknown date and place.

name: Luna 9
short_status: Landed in Oceanus Procellarum 3 Feb 1966, transmitted until 6 Feb 1966; exact resting place still unconfirmed as of July 2026, with two rival candidate sites identified in early 2026.

name: Lunar Orbiter Program
short_status: Five orbiters flown 1966 to 1967, all five successful; each was deliberately crashed into the Moon at the end of its mission, the last on January 31, 1968.

name: Surveyor 1
short_status: First US soft lunar landing, June 2, 1966, Oceanus Procellarum; operated until final contact on January 7, 1967.

name: Surveyor 2 to 7
short_status: Six-mission conclusion of the US Surveyor program, Sep 1966 to Feb 1968: four soft-landed (Surveyors 3, 5, 6, 7), two failed (2 crashed, 4 vanished). Apollo 12 later visited Surveyor 3, the only robotic craft humans have ever returned to.

name: Apollo 8
short_status: Completed Dec 27, 1968: first crewed flight to leave Earth orbit, 10 lunar orbits on Christmas Eve, recovered by USS Yorktown in the Pacific.

name: Zond 5
short_status: Uncrewed circumlunar flight, Sep 14-21, 1968: first spacecraft (and first Earth life, two steppe tortoises) to loop around the Moon and return safely to Earth.

name: Apollo 10
short_status: Completed May 26, 1969: full dress rehearsal for the Moon landing; LM Snoopy flew to roughly 47,400 ft above the surface, clearing the way for Apollo 11.

name: Apollo 11
short_status: Success: first crewed lunar landing, July 20, 1969, 20:17:40 UTC at Tranquility Base; crew returned to Earth July 24, 1969.

name: Apollo 12
short_status: Second crewed Moon landing. Intrepid touched down 19 Nov 1969 in Oceanus Procellarum, about 160 m (535 ft) from the Surveyor 3 probe. Crew returned 24 Nov 1969. Success.

name: Luna 15
short_status: Failure: crashed in Mare Crisium on 21 July 1969 at about 15:50 UT, roughly two hours before Apollo 11 lifted off from the Moon, ending the Soviet attempt to return lunar soil before the Americans got home.

name: Apollo 13
short_status: Aborted Moon landing, April 11-17, 1970: oxygen tank rupture about 200,000 miles out; all three crew returned safely. NASA's "successful failure".

name: Luna 16
short_status: Success: returned 101 g of Mare Fecunditatis soil, 12 to 24 September 1970, the first robotic sample return from another world.

name: Luna 17 / Lunokhod 1
short_status: Success: landed 17 November 1970; Lunokhod 1 became the first rover on another world, drove ~10 km over 11 lunar days, and its laser reflector has been answering Earth again since 2010.

name: Apollo 14
short_status: Third crewed Moon landing. Antares set down 5 Feb 1971 at Fra Mauro (Apollo 13's lost target). Shepard and Mitchell logged 9h23m of EVA; returned 9 Feb 1971. Success.

name: Apollo 15
short_status: Landed at Hadley-Apennine July 30, 1971; splashed down Aug 7, 1971; its laser retroreflector is still Earth's primary lunar ranging target (as of 2026).

name: Luna 18 and Luna 23
short_status: Failure: two Soviet sample-return attempts that brought back nothing. Luna 18 crashed near Mare Fecunditatis on 11 Sep 1971; Luna 23 tipped onto its side landing in Mare Crisium on 6 Nov 1974 and wrecked its brand-new deep drill, though it kept transmitting for 3 days.

name: Apollo 16
short_status: Landed in the Descartes Highlands April 20, 1972; splashed down April 27, 1972 after a mission cut one day short.

name: Apollo 17
short_status: Landed at Taurus-Littrow December 11, 1972; last crewed Moon landing, splashed down December 19, 1972.

name: Luna 20
short_status: Success: returned about 55 g from the Apollonius highlands, 14 to 25 February 1972, the first sample of lunar highland soil brought back by a robot.

name: Luna 21 / Lunokhod 2
short_status: Success: landed in Le Monnier crater on 15 January 1973; Lunokhod 2 drove about 39 km over four lunar days, an off-world distance record that stood until 2014, and its French-built reflector is still ranged from Earth.

name: Luna 24
short_status: Success: returned 170.1 g from Mare Crisium, 9 to 22 August 1976; the last Soviet lunar mission, and the last lunar samples anyone returned for 44 years.

name: Hiten (MUSES-A)
short_status: Deliberately impacted the Moon between Stevinus and Furnerius Apr 10, 1993 (Apr 11 JST); Uesugi 1996 records two impact solutions, 18:03:25.7 UT at 34.0 S, 55.3 E and 18:08:45 UT at 34.3 S, 55.6 E. Hagoromo's lunar orbit was never confirmed.

name: Clementine
short_status: Mapped the whole Moon Feb 26 to Apr 22, 1994 (297 orbits, about 1.6 million images); left lunar orbit May 3, 1994; a thruster fault on May 7 ended the Geographos flyby plan; mission terminated Aug 8, 1994.

name: Lunar Prospector
short_status: Impacted Shoemaker crater near the lunar south pole July 31, 1999, ending 18 months of mapping; the hoped-for water plume never appeared, and the crater now bears the name of the man whose ashes it holds.

name: SMART-1
short_status: Impacted the Moon Sep 3, 2006: last signal 05:42:22 UT from Lacus Excellentiae; the infrared flash was recorded from Hawaii, and LRO images located the 4 by 20 m impact gouge in 2017.

name: Chang'e 1
short_status: Controlled impact in Mare Fecunditatis Mar 1, 2009, 08:13 UTC, after 16 months in orbit; the impact scar was later identified in LROC images at 1.66 S, 52.27 E (Icarus, 2019).

name: Kaguya (SELENE)
short_status: Controlled impact near Gill crater Jun 10, 2009, 18:25 UT, after about 20 months at the Moon; subsatellite Okina impacted the far side Feb 12, 2009; Ouna was left in lunar orbit at the end of its mission.

name: Chandrayaan-1
short_status: Mission ended Aug 29, 2009 (IST) when contact was lost 312 days in, with about 95% of objectives met; JPL ground radar located the derelict orbiter still circling at about 200 km in 2016-17.

name: LCROSS
short_status: Impacted Cabeus crater Oct 9, 2009; water ice confirmed Nov 13, 2009, quantified at 155 kg in the plume (Science, Oct 2010).

name: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)
short_status: Operating: more than 17 years in lunar orbit (NASA, September 16, 2026), now in its sixth extended science mission (October 2025 through September 2028).

name: Chang'e 2
short_status: Mapped the Moon at 7 m through 2011, reached Sun-Earth L2, flew by asteroid Toutatis Dec 13, 2012; contact faded after 2014, now a silent derelict in solar orbit.

name: ARTEMIS P1 and P2
short_status: Operating: 15 years in lunar orbit, with fresh magnetometer files from both probes on Berkeley's public data server through October 24, 2026 (as of October 26, 2026).

name: GRAIL (Ebb and Flow)
short_status: Complete: twin orbiters mapped the Moon's gravity through 2012, then struck a far-northern mountain on Dec 17, 2012; NASA named the site for Sally Ride.

name: Chang'e 3 and Yutu
short_status: Landed Dec 14, 2013 in Mare Imbrium; Yutu operated 972 days to Jul 31, 2016; lander signals still confirmed Dec 31, 2025

name: LADEE
short_status: Impacted the lunar far side near Sundman V crater April 18, 2014 (04:30-05:22 UTC window); LROC located the sub-3 m crater in October 2014.

name: Chang'e 5-T1 (Xiaofei)
short_status: Circumlunar free-return flight test, 23 to 31 October 2014: the Xiaofei capsule proved the high-speed skip reentry for Chang'e 5 and landed in Inner Mongolia; the service module flew on to Earth-Moon L2 and then into lunar orbit.

name: Queqiao-1 and the Longjiang microsatellites
short_status: Launched 20 May 2018 as three spacecraft: Queqiao-1 reached the Earth-Moon L2 halo orbit and relayed Chang'e 4 for over five years (relay duty handed to Queqiao-2 in 2024); Longjiang-2 succeeded and was deliberately impacted 31 Jul 2019; Longjiang-1 failed to reach lunar orbit.

name: Chandrayaan-2
short_status: Partial: the Vikram lander crashed during descent on Sep 6, 2019 (UTC); the orbiter is still operating in its ~100 km polar orbit as of July 2026, in its seventh year on a one-year design life.

name: Chang'e 4 (Yutu-2 rover and Queqiao-1 relay)
short_status: Landed Jan 3, 2019 in Von Kármán crater, first-ever far-side landing; lander and Yutu-2 last officially reported working in Sep 2024, Yutu-2 largely stationary since Mar 2024 with last official odometer 1,613 m (no later official status found as of Sep 28, 2026)

name: Chang'e 5
short_status: Returned 1,731 g from Oceanus Procellarum on Dec 16, 2020; orbiter flew on and was still operating in lunar distant retrograde orbit per April 2025 reporting.

name: WE0913A (2022 rocket body)
short_status: Hit the far side on Mar 4, 2022 and left a double crater, 18 m and 16 m wide, imaged by LRO at 5.226 N, 234.486 E. First identified as a SpaceX stage, later reattributed to a Chinese booster; officially it remains unattributed.

name: Chandrayaan-3
short_status: Landed 23 Aug 2023 at 69.37 S (Statio Shiv Shakti); Vikram and Pragyan completed one lunar day plus a hop bonus, the propulsion module returned to Earth orbit; full success.

name: Lunar Gateway
operator: NASA-led with ESA, JAXA, CSA, MBRSC (UAE)
short_status: Paused in its current form since Mar 24, 2026; HALO under stop-work, PPE repurposed for the SR-1 Freedom Mars mission, partners re-planning (as of Jul 18, 2026)

name: Beresheet
short_status: Crashed on Mare Serenitatis during landing on 11 Apr 2019; reached lunar orbit but a reset command to a failed IMU cut the main engine. First privately funded lunar landing attempt.

name: Beresheet 2
short_status: Engineering frozen since April 2025 for lack of funding, and described by SpaceIL as a freeze rather than a cancellation. The follow-up to the crashed Beresheet was designed as one orbiter and two small landers on a single launch, but has no active schedule as of October 2026.

name: International Lunar Research Station (ILRS)
short_status: In development: 13 national members as of July 2026; Chang'e-7 precursor launch postponed on 23 Aug 2026 with no new date announced (as of 2 Nov 2026); basic station targeted 2035 at the lunar south pole.

name: Artemis I CubeSats
operator: Ten secondary payloads (NASA, JAXA, ASI/Argotec, universities and companies)
short_status: Partial. Ten shoebox-sized CubeSats rode Artemis I into deep space on 16 November 2022; three worked as intended (ArgoMoon, BioSentinel, EQUULEUS), LunIR half-worked as a technology demo, and the other six were lost or crippled, several by batteries that drained flat during 13 months of launch delays.

name: CAPSTONE
short_status: All primary and extended mission objectives achieved; NASA activities concluded June 2026 after nearly four years; Advanced Space continues flying it as a commercial testbed in the NRHO (as of July 2026).

name: Danuri (Korea Pathfinder Lunar Orbiter)
short_status: Operating: in a 60 x 200 km frozen orbit since September 24, 2025, twice extended through December 2027 as of July 2026; a controlled lunar impact is planned for March 2028.

name: China's Crewed Lunar Program
short_status: In development: first crewed landing targeted before 2030 (restated by CMSA May 23, 2026); CZ-10A/Mengzhou-1 orbital debut listed by CMSA among its 2026 flights (Nov 2025), though CMSA's Feb 27, 2026 annual plan does not name it and no date has been given; trackers report a slip to 2027 and CMSA has announced no change (as of Nov 2, 2026); CZ-10B variant flew and was recovered Jul 10, 2026; an uncrewed Lanyue lander flight is planned before the crewed landing (CMSA, Oct 22, 2026), and on Oct 31, 2026 CCTV, reporting from CMSA's academic conference, said uncrewed Mengzhou and Lanyue flights are both planned ahead of the crewed landing; no dates given.

name: ispace Hakuto-R Missions 1 and 2
short_status: Two landing attempts, Apr 25, 2023 (Atlas crater) and Jun 5, 2025 UTC (Mare Frigoris), both crashed; next ispace landing targeted 2028 on the new ULTRA lander (as of Jul 2026).

name: Luna 25
short_status: Crashed into the Moon 19 Aug 2023 after an orbit-lowering burn ran 43 seconds long; NASA's LRO photographed the ~10 m crater on 24 Aug 2023.

name: Chang'e 6 and Queqiao-2
short_status: Success: first-ever far-side sample return. 1,935.3 g landed in Inner Mongolia on Jun 25, 2024; Queqiao-2 relay still operating, sample science running hot through 2026.

name: IM-1 Odysseus
operator: Intuitive Machines (US, commercial, flying NASA CLPS payloads)
short_status: Landed at 80.13°S near Malapert A on Feb 22, 2024; tipped ~30°, transmitted until Feb 29, 2024; did not survive lunar night (confirmed Mar 23, 2024).

name: Peregrine Mission One
operator: Astrobotic (US, commercial, flying NASA CLPS payloads)
short_status: Launched Jan 8, 2024 on Vulcan's first flight; a helium-valve failure hours later ruled out landing; controlled South Pacific reentry Jan 18, 2024.

name: SLIM (Smart Lander for Investigating Moon)
short_status: Landed Jan 20, 2024 (JST): world's first pinpoint lunar landing (~10 m vs 100 m goal); survived three lunar nights; operations ended Aug 23, 2024.

name: Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1
short_status: Success: landed upright in Mare Crisium Mar 2, 2025; 14 days of surface ops with 10 NASA payloads; mission concluded Mar 16, 2025.

name: Intuitive Machines IM-2 (Athena)
short_status: Partial: landed on its side in a crater on Mons Mouton Mar 6, 2025 (southernmost lunar landing); mission ended Mar 7, 2025 after about 13 hours.

name: Falcon 9 upper stage (2025-010D)
short_status: Hit the Moon on Aug 5, 2026 near Einstein crater: the spent second stage from the Falcon 9 that launched Blue Ghost 1 and Resilience in Jan 2025. Unintentional. LRO photographed the crater on Aug 11-12 and measured it at about 60 feet (18 m) across and under 10 feet (3 m) deep, centred at 19.4759 N, 266.7138 E.

name: Griffin Mission One
operator: Astrobotic (US, commercial; renamed Voyager Lunar Systems after Voyager Technologies' acquisition closed Jul 13, 2026)
short_status: Flight lander built, unveiled Jun 15, 2026, and finished acceptance testing at NASA JPL (NASA and Voyager, Oct 13, 2026); now back in Pittsburgh for final assembly before shipment to Cape Canaveral, with a Falcon Heavy launch targeted for late 2026 (as of Nov 2, 2026).

name: Blue Moon Mark 1
short_status: In development, waiting on its rocket: pathfinder Endurance is fully assembled and thermal-vacuum tested, with a cryogenic propellant-loading test next, but the May 28, 2026 New Glenn pad explosion pushed its debut to early 2027 (NASA and Blue Origin, Sep 15, 2026); VIPER rides a second MK1, targeted for 2027 (NASA, Oct 20, 2026).

name: Chang'e 7
short_status: Launch postponed: on 23 Aug 2026 the China Manned Space Engineering Office said Chang'e 7 does not meet the conditions for launch and cannot fly in this year's scheduled window. No Chinese official source has given a new date or a reason; partner agencies say 2027 (as of 2 Nov 2026).

name: Chandrayaan-4
short_status: In development, not launched: Cabinet-approved Sep 18, 2024 (Rs 2,104.06 crore); launch targeted by 2028 (as of July 2026), with an April 2026 parliamentary review flagging launch-vehicle readiness as the pacing risk.

name: LUPEX (Lunar Polar Exploration)
short_status: In development, not launched: India's government cleared its share on March 10, 2025 and the two agencies signed the implementing arrangement on August 29, 2025; joint design work is underway (fifth technical interface meeting, December 2025) with launch targeted no earlier than 2028, which JAXA's Japanese page gives as Japanese fiscal year 2028, April 2028 to March 2029 (as of Oct 2026). No landing site fixed yet.

name: Chang'e 8
short_status: In development: CNSA's published target is a launch around 2029 to the Leibnitz-Beta Plateau (Mons Mouton) with an ISRU lunar-brick 3D-printing demo. SpaceNews reported on 10 Sep 2026 that China appears to be reconfiguring its robotic Moon program, Chang'e 8 included; no Chinese official source has announced a change (as of 2 Nov 2026).

name: Artemis I
short_status: Flown: uncrewed lunar test flight, November to December 2022

name: Artemis II
short_status: Flown: crewed lunar flyby, 1 to 10 April 2026

name: Artemis III
short_status: Announced: crewed low Earth orbit demonstration, targeted 2027 (as of 2 November 2026)

name: Artemis IV
short_status: Announced: first crewed lunar landing, targeted early 2028 (as of 2 November 2026)

name: Artemis V
short_status: Announced: lunar surface mission, anticipated by late 2028 (as of 2 November 2026); no crew or lander assigned

name: Mars 1M No. 1 and No. 2
short_status: Two spacecraft, two launch failures, on 10 and 14 October 1960. Neither reached Earth orbit, and the USSR never acknowledged either flight; almost everything known about them comes from Western tracking and from post-Soviet memoirs.

name: Sputnik 22, Mars 1 and Sputnik 24
short_status: Three launches, 24 October to 4 November 1962: two never left Earth orbit and were never announced. The third, Mars 1, lost its attitude control gas within days and fell silent on 21 March 1963 at 106 million km.

name: Mariner 3
short_status: Killed by its own nose cone on 5 November 1964: the payload shroud never separated, the solar panels could not open, and the batteries died 8 hours 43 minutes after liftoff. Silent in solar orbit ever since.

name: Zond 2
short_status: Crippled hours after launch on 30 November 1964 by a jammed solar panel, on about half power, it fired the first electric thrusters beyond Earth orbit, went silent by May 1965 and passed Mars unheard on 6 August 1965.

name: Zond 3
short_status: Success: launched 18 July 1965 towards the orbit of Mars with no Mars at the end of it, it photographed the unseen third of the lunar far side and replayed those frames to 153.5 million km by March 1966.

name: Mariner 4
short_status: Flew 9,846 km above Mars at 01:00:57 UTC on 15 July 1965 and returned the first close-up photographs of another planet. Communications were terminated 21 December 1967; the spacecraft is derelict in solar orbit.

name: The Soviet crewed Mars programme
short_status: Cancelled, and never built. Design ran at OKB-1 from 1959, was halted by decree on 13 May 1961, continued anyway, was revived in 1969 as Aelita and died with the N1; the only hardware was a Moscow mock-up.

name: Voyager (Mars)
short_status: Cancelled at the end of August 1967, when Congress zeroed its fiscal 1968 appropriation: seven years of study and no flight hardware. The orbiter-and-lander architecture went into Viking, which landed on Mars in 1976.

name: Mars Excursion Module
short_status: Never built, and never formally cancelled: no crewed Mars programme was ever approved for it to belong to. It was designed three times between 1963 and 1967, by Philco Aeronutronic, Marshall and North American Rockwell.

name: Mars 4NM and 5NM
short_status: Never built: both flights died with the N1, which failed on all four of its test launches. Designed at Lavochkin from 1970, 4NM would have landed a rover and 5NM flown 200 g of Martian soil home.

name: Mariner 6 and 7
short_status: Both flybys succeeded: Mariner 6 passed Mars on 31 July 1969 and Mariner 7 on 5 August 1969 UTC, returning 201 pictures between them. Both fell silent in the early 1970s and remain derelict in solar orbit.

name: Mars 1969A and 1969B
short_status: Two identical Soviet Mars orbiters, both destroyed by their Proton rockets six days apart in spring 1969. Neither reached Earth orbit, and the USSR never acknowledged that they existed.

name: PrOP-M
short_status: Both lost without ever moving: two 4.5 kg ski-walking robots rode to Mars in 1971. The first was destroyed when Mars 2 hit the ground on 27 November; Mars 3 landed on 2 December and fell silent within two minutes.

name: Kosmos 419
short_status: Reached Earth parking orbit on 10 May 1971, but its Blok D upper stage never restarted because the wrong ignition time had been loaded into the onboard computer. It reentered on 12 May 1971.

name: Mariner 8
short_status: Lost on 9 May 1971 when the Centaur upper stage lost pitch control about 4.7 minutes after liftoff. It fell into the Atlantic, and its mapping mission was folded into Mariner 9.

name: Mariner 9
short_status: Success: the first spacecraft to orbit another planet, arriving 14 November 1971 UTC and commanded off on 27 October 1972 after 348 days and 7,329 pictures. Presumed still in Mars orbit, no re-entry confirmed as of 24 September 2026.

name: Mars 2
short_status: Crashed on 27 November 1971, the first human-made object to reach the surface of Mars; the orbiter it rode on flew 362 orbits before the mission was declared over on 22 August 1972. The wreck has never been located.

name: Mars 3
short_status: First confirmed soft landing on Mars, at about 13:50:35 UT on 2 December 1971. It began transmitting 90 seconds later and stopped almost immediately; how long it spoke and why it stopped are still unsettled in 2026.

name: Mars 4, 5, 6 and 7
short_status: None of the four 1973 probes completed its mission: Mars 4 flew past without braking, Mars 5 leaked air in orbit, Mars 7 missed the planet, and Mars 6 sent the first data from inside the atmosphere on 12 March 1974.

name: Mars 5M
short_status: Cancelled with flight vehicles already in manufacture. Russian sources close this Soviet sample return on 17 November 1977, the week its chief designer lost his job; Perminov, who worked on it, dates the end to 1978.

name: The Viking biology results
short_status: All three Viking life-detection experiments returned signals in 1976. As of 24 September 2026 most of the field explains them by soil chemistry, one control still has no reproduced chemical explanation, and the case is open.

name: Viking 1
short_status: Landed in western Chryse Planitia on 20 July 1976 and worked 2,245 sols against a 90-day design life. Killed on 19 November 1982 by a command from Earth that overwrote its antenna-pointing memory.

name: Viking 2
short_status: Landed in Utopia Planitia on 3 September 1976, canted 8.2 degrees with one footpad on a rock, and worked 1,281 sols against a 90-day design life. Turned off on 11 April 1980 when its batteries stopped holding a charge.

name: Mars 94 and Mars 98
operator: USSR and Russia (IKI, NPO Lavochkin, VNIITransmash), with CNES and NASA
short_status: Five efforts, one launch. Vesta never became hardware, Mars 94 lost its twin in 1991 and then its 1994 launch date, and Mars 98 was closed in the spring of 1995; the surviving airframe flew as Mars 96 in November 1996.

name: Mars Aerostat
operator: CNES and IKI (France, USSR then Russia)
short_status: Terminated in 1995 over money, with hardware built and tested on Earth. No balloon has ever been released at Mars; only its relay receiver flew, on Mars Observer in 1992 and Mars Global Surveyor in 1996.

name: The sample returns cancelled before this one
short_status: Two American sample returns died before hardware. Mars Rover/Sample Return went with the Space Exploration Initiative in 1990, and the NASA and CNES project promising samples in October 2008 fell after the 1999 losses.

name: Phobos 1 and 2
short_status: Both spacecraft died before the landings they were built for: Phobos 1 on 31 August 1988, killed by a single missing character in an uploaded command, and Phobos 2 on 27 March 1989, after 57 days in Mars orbit.

name: Space Exploration Initiative: the Mars element
short_status: Politically dead within eleven months of President George H. W. Bush announcing it on 20 July 1989: the House Appropriations Committee deleted every SEI budget line on 26 June 1990. No Mars hardware was ever built.

name: The Mars networks that were never built
short_status: No network of small stations has ever landed on Mars. At least five were designed in detail between 1991 and 2004, MESUR, INTERMARSNET, NetLander, Pascal and MetNet, and every one was cancelled for money.

name: Mars Observer
short_status: Lost on 22 August 1993 during a planned fourteen-minute radio blackout, 68 hours short of Mars orbit insertion. The failure board found no smoking gun, and whether the spacecraft reached orbit is still unknown.

name: Mars Surveyor Program
short_status: Two of the four spacecraft flown worked, Mars Global Surveyor and the orbiter renamed 2001 Mars Odyssey; Mars Climate Orbiter and Mars Polar Lander were both lost in 1999. NASA replaced the programme on 26 October 2000.

name: Mars Surveyor 2001 Lander
short_status: Built and never flown: NASA said on 28 March 2000 that it was cancelled and on hold indefinitely, a near copy of Mars Polar Lander, which had crashed on 3 December 1999. Its structure reached Mars in 2008 as Phoenix.

name: Mars 96
short_status: Never left Earth orbit: the Blok D-2 missed its second burn and Mars 96 re-entered on 17 November 1996 over the eastern Pacific, Chile and Bolivia. Nothing was recovered, including about 270 g of plutonium-238.

name: Mars Global Surveyor
short_status: Mapped Mars for nine years, more than four times its planned mission. Last contact 2 November 2006, after a memory write sent in June drove a solar array into its hard stop and left the antenna pointing away from Earth.

name: Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner
short_status: Success: bounced into Ares Vallis on airbags on 4 July 1997 and put the first wheels on Mars two days later. Last data came 27 September 1997; NASA stopped calling on 10 March 1998, and HiRISE found the lander in 2006.

name: Mars Micromissions and the Kitty Hawk airplane
short_status: No micromission was ever built. NASA and CNES planned 220 kg spacecraft riding Ariane 5 for free to build a six-satellite Mars relay network, starting in 2003 with either a relay orbiter or an aeroplane.

name: Nozomi
short_status: Japan's first mission to another planet, and it never reached Mars orbit: a valve in the oxidiser feed failed on 20 December 1998, insertion was abandoned on 9 December 2003, and Nozomi passed Mars at about 1,000 km.

name: Deep Space 2
short_status: Neither probe was ever heard from after 3 December 1999, and nothing confirms Amundsen and Scott separated, entered or reached the ground. The review board named no probable cause, only four plausible failure modes.

name: Mars Climate Orbiter
short_status: Lost at orbit insertion on 23 September 1999: the carrier vanished 49 seconds early and never returned. One root cause, a ground file giving thruster impulse in pound-force seconds where newton-seconds were specified.

name: Mars Polar Lander
short_status: Lost on 3 December 1999 with no descent telemetry, and never found. The review board's probable cause is a spurious touchdown signal at leg deployment that shut the engine off at about 40 m.

name: Life detection: the missions NASA did not fly
short_status: One life-detection payload has flown to Mars, Viking's in 1976. The Astrobiology Field Laboratory and Icebreaker were studied and never started, and as of September 2026 the next Discovery call is not expected before 2028.

name: ARES, the Mars airplane
short_status: Never built beyond subscale test articles. NASA Langley's rocket-powered aeroplane, designed for a single 70-minute flight over the Southern Highlands, lost Mars Scout to Phoenix in 2003 and was passed over in 2007.

name: The Phobos and Deimos missions that were never flown
short_status: Between 1997 and 2018 at least ten serious proposals to visit Phobos or Deimos were made, and none was selected for flight. Aladdin came closest, twice a Discovery finalist; Japan's MMX, chosen outside that process, launched on 20 October 2026.

name: The Mars hardware with no ride
operator: Finnish Meteorological Institute, Lavochkin, INTA, Thoth Technology, NASA/JPL
short_status: Built and tested from the mid-1990s to 2020, then never launched: as of 24 August 2026 none of this hardware has left Earth. Two flight-capable MetNet landers existed by September 2013 with no rocket bought for them.

name: The Mars Scout Program
short_status: Ended without a third competition: two missions were selected, Phoenix in 2003 and MAVEN in 2008, and NASA opened Discovery to Mars in 2010. Both have now finished, MAVEN declared unrecoverable on 3 June 2026.

name: 2001 Mars Odyssey
short_status: Operating as of 28 October 2026, four days after its 25th anniversary in Mars orbit: NASA's Deep Space Network was receiving its telemetry that day. It has orbited Mars since 24 October 2001, longer than any other spacecraft, and still relays rover data. NASA's 2025 Senior Review put its usable propellant at 3.2 kg, give or take 2 kg.

name: Beagle 2
short_status: Landed on Isidis Planitia on 25 December 2003, never sent a single bit, and was declared lost on 6 February 2004. HiRISE found it intact on 16 January 2015, panels only partly opened; still silent as of 23 August 2026.

name: Mars Express
short_status: Operating as of 24 September 2026: Europe's first mission to another planet has orbited Mars since 25 December 2003. It carried the lost Beagle 2, and its MARSIS radar found the most argued-over reflection on Mars.

name: Mars Telecommunications Orbiter
short_status: Cancelled on 21 July 2005 before construction, and nothing replaced it. NASA sought proposals for a commercially built Mars Telecommunications Network on 14 May 2026, with no award announced as of 24 August 2026.

name: Opportunity (MER-B)
short_status: Landed in Eagle crater on 25 January 2004 for a 90-sol mission and worked 5,111 sols, driving 45.16 km. A planet-encircling dust storm ended it: last signal 10 June 2018, mission complete 13 February 2019.

name: Spirit (MER-A)
short_status: Landed in Gusev Crater on 4 January 2004 for a 90-sol mission and worked 2,210 sols. Its last downlink came on 22 March 2010; NASA closed the recovery on 25 May 2011, and nothing had answered by 23 August 2026.

name: The place names of Mars
short_status: Operating as of 24 August 2026: the IAU gazetteer holds 2,052 approved names on Mars and not one is a landing site. Bradbury Landing, Wright Brothers Field and the memorial stations are agency names only.

name: World Trade Center Aluminium on Mars
short_status: Still on Mars: aluminium from the World Trade Center site, machined into the rock abrasion tool cable shield on each of Spirit and Opportunity, rovers that fell silent in March 2010 and June 2018.

name: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter
short_status: Operating as of 28 October 2026, when NASA's Deep Space Network was taking its downlink at 2 Mbit/s. In Mars orbit since 10 March 2006 and now in its twenty-first year, it is still relaying and still imaging. CRISM is dead; HiRISE and the Mars Climate Sounder are damaged but working.

name: Mars-500, SIRIUS and CHAPEA
operator: Institute of Biomedical Problems, Moscow, with ESA, China and NASA
short_status: Completed: six men sealed into chambers in Moscow for 520 days, 3 June 2010 to 4 November 2011. The line runs on through Russia's SIRIUS series to NASA's CHAPEA, whose second crew is due out on 31 October 2026.

name: MAX-C and the Mars Exploration Joint Initiative
short_status: Never built: NASA's caching rover concept of 2009, meant to launch in May 2018 beside Europe's ExoMars rover, was merged away in April 2011 on cost. The caching idea survived and became Perseverance.

name: MELOS
short_status: Closed without ever becoming a mission: a Japanese working group approved in June 2008 and terminated by a report submitted on 25 December 2014. Its final rover proposal lost the medium-class call of 16 February 2015.

name: Phoenix
short_status: Landed 25 May 2008 at 68.22 N in the Martian arctic, touched and analysed water ice and measured 0.4 to 0.6 percent perchlorate in the soil. Last signal 2 November 2008; NASA formally ended the mission on 24 May 2010.

name: Visions of Mars
operator: The Planetary Society, with IKI and NASA
short_status: On Mars since 25 May 2008 and still unread: a Planetary Society disc of about 80 Mars works, bolted to the Phoenix lander deck at 68.22 N, 234.25 E. The first copy was lost with Mars 96 in November 1996.

name: Phobos-Grunt and Yinghuo-1
short_status: Stranded in low Earth orbit after launch on 8 November 2011: neither Mars burn ever fired, and the stack re-entered over the Pacific on 15 January 2012 with China's Yinghuo-1 still attached.

name: Red Dragon
operator: SpaceX with NASA Ames Research Center (United States)
short_status: Cancelled on 19 July 2017, when Musk dropped propulsive landing for Dragon: the capsule was to land on Mars on its own engines with no parachute, announced by SpaceX on 27 April 2016. None was ever built.

name: Curiosity (Mars Science Laboratory)
short_status: Operating as of 27 October 2026: fourteen years and past 5,000 Martian days, a milestone NASA's Curiosity blog dates to Saturday 29 August 2026, on a mission whose prime phase was one Martian year. The newest waypoint in NASA's MMGIS traverse file, last modified 16 October 2026, is sol 5045, a 12.64 m drive, with a cumulative drive distance of 38,480.16 m in that file's dist_total_m field, against 38.16 in the same record's dist_km field. NASA's raw images through sol 5056 (27 October 2026) show the rover at the same position.

name: Mars One
operator: Mars One Foundation (Netherlands) and Mars One Ventures AG (Switzerland)
short_status: Cancelled: a one-way Mars settlement announced in 2012 for a 2023 landing, funded by broadcast rights. Nothing was built, and a Basel court declared the for-profit arm, Mars One Ventures AG, bankrupt on 15 January 2019.

name: Inspiration Mars
short_status: Never flew: Dennis Tito's 2013 plan to loop two people past Mars on a 501-day free return from 5 January 2018. NASA declined his 700 million dollar request in November 2013 and the foundation's website went dark in late 2015.

name: Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan)
short_status: Lost after a long eclipse in April 2022; ISRO declared it non-recoverable on 27 September 2022. First Asian spacecraft to orbit Mars, it arrived in September 2014 and worked eight years against a six-month design life.

name: MAVEN
short_status: Declared unrecoverable on 3 June 2026, after eleven years in Mars orbit against a one-year primary science mission. Its last signal came on 6 December 2025 and why it started spinning is still unexplained.

name: ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter
short_status: Operating as of 28 October 2026. On 27 October ESA published attitude data taken from the spacecraft's telemetry through 24 October 2026, and raw ACS, NOMAD and FREND products in ESA's public archive run to 29 May 2026.

name: Schiaparelli EDM
short_status: Destroyed on impact in Meridiani Planum on 19 October 2016 at 14:47:28 UTC, 37 seconds early, at about 150 m/s. ESA's inquiry board reported on 17 April 2017 and ESA announced the findings on 24 May 2017.

name: InSight
short_status: Ended on 15 December 2022, four years after landing in Elysium Planitia, when dust cut its solar power by about ninety per cent. It left 1,319 marsquakes, the first seismic catalogue of a planet other than Earth.

name: MarCO A and B
short_status: In orbit around the Sun and silent since 4 January 2019. The two CubeSats relayed InSight's landing live from about 3,500 km out on 26 November 2018, then stopped answering within six weeks.

name: The HP3 Mole
short_status: Failed: abandoned on 9 January 2021 at a tip depth of 37 cm against a 3 m minimum, so the heat flow measurement was never made. The mole is intact, wholly underground in Elysium Planitia and tilted about 30 degrees.

name: Mars gravity assists
short_status: Five spacecraft have bent their trajectories at Mars: Rosetta in 2007, Dawn in 2009, Europa Clipper and Hera in March 2025 and Psyche on 15 May 2026. Three of the five fell inside fourteen and a half months.

name: Mars as an observatory
short_status: Twice the Mars fleet has been turned round to look outward: at comet Siding Spring on 19 October 2014 and at 3I/ATLAS in October 2025, whose predicted position the Mars astrometry then improved tenfold.

name: Kazachok
short_status: Built, tested, mated to the rover and never launched. ESA suspended the ExoMars cooperation with Roscosmos on 17 March 2022 and terminated it in July; Roscosmos said the platform was home in Russia on 30 October 2024.

name: International Mars Ice Mapper
operator: NASA, CSA, JAXA and ASI, later joined by the Netherlands Space Office
short_status: NASA terminated its financial support on 28 March 2022 and the other partners did not follow: Italy signed a 22 million euro Phase B1 contract on 8 March 2024. As of 24 August 2026 no agency has said whether it lives.

name: The deleted Mars Sample Return vehicles
short_status: None reached a launch pad. From 2022 the campaign deleted its fetch rover, a second lander, two helicopters and the ascent vehicle, and ESA members asked to cancel the Earth Return Orbiter, reported on 28 March 2026.

name: Tianwen-1's deployable cameras
short_status: Success: three throwaway cameras, one ejected on the cruise in 2020, one reported released in Mars orbit at the end of 2021, and the one Zhurong dropped on 1 June 2021 for the portrait, still lying in Utopia Planitia.

name: Hope (Emirates Mars Mission)
operator: MBRSC and UAE Space Agency (United Arab Emirates)
short_status: In Mars orbit since 9 February 2021 and still flying as of 23 August 2026: the UAE announced a three-year extension to 2028 on 17 February 2026, and JPL held tracking data for it through 28 May 2026.

name: Ingenuity
short_status: Grounded at Valinor Hills since 18 January 2024, when all four rotor blades broke on landing. NASA declared the mission complete on 25 January 2024 and left it recording with no way to send anything home.

name: Messages to Mars
short_status: The deliberate messages are still there, from a Soviet pennant that arrived as wreckage on 27 November 1971 to flags, memorial plaques, four sundials, a 1909 penny and a parachute encoding DARE MIGHTY THINGS. One plaque meant for Mars is still in a museum in Washington.

name: Perseverance (Mars 2020)
short_status: Operating as of 26 October 2026, and the record holder for distance driven on another world. On sol 2006, 11 October 2026, a 91.31 m drive took its odometer to 45.22 km, past the 45.16 km Opportunity set, and JPL announced the record the next day. NASA's raw-image feed carries pictures taken through sol 2020, the latest at 05:30 UTC on 26 October 2026, and its traverse file, last modified 15 October 2026, ends on sol 2009 at 45,223.649 m.

name: Send Your Name to Mars
short_status: Seven spacecraft have put about 22.9 million name entries on the Martian surface, from Pathfinder in 1997 to Perseverance's 10,932,295 in 2021. NASA's page, updated 27 July 2026, says reservations are closed.

name: The Mars Microphone
short_status: Working since February 2021 on Perseverance, at the third attempt: NASA was still publishing new SuperCam audio in August 2026. The first was lost with Mars Polar Lander in 1999, the second never ran on Phoenix.

name: Tianwen-1
short_status: The orbiter is still working: CNSA said on 20 May 2026 that it is running stably. It reached Mars orbit on 10 February 2021 and landed Zhurong on 14 May 2021; the rover has been silent since May 2022.

name: Zhurong
short_status: Silent since 18 May 2022, when it hibernated for the Martian winter after 358 sols and 1,921 m against a design life of 90. Dust is the likely cause, and as of 24 September 2026 China has declared no formal end.

name: The Three Forks sample depot
short_status: Intact and uncollected: ten sealed titanium tubes Perseverance laid on the floor of Jezero Crater between 21 December 2022 and 28 January 2023. As of 3 September 2026 no mission is scheduled to retrieve them.

name: Hera at Deimos
short_status: Success: Hera photographed the far side of Deimos from about 1,000 km on 12 March 2025 during a Mars gravity assist. In August 2026 those frames pinned a Nature Astronomy reconstruction to a 320 m impactor.

name: ESCAPADE
operator: NASA / UC Berkeley Space Sciences Laboratory / Rocket Lab
short_status: Operating as of 28 October 2026: both orbiters are being tracked, Blue 1.04 million km and Gold 1.16 million km from Earth and falling back towards it, loitering since their 13 November 2025 launch. The burns for Mars are planned for 7 November (Blue) and 9 November (Gold), arrival September 2027.

name: Idefix (MMX Phobos rover)
operator: CNES and DLR, flying with JAXA
short_status: Launched on 20 October 2026, stowed on JAXA's MMX, which lifted off at 04:41:03 Japan time (19:41:03 UTC on 19 October) on H3 flight 10. JAXA reported the spacecraft healthy on 21 October. Release onto Phobos from 40 to 100 metres up is planned for late 2028 or 2029.

name: Martian Moons eXploration (MMX)
short_status: Operating as of 28 October 2026: MMX lifted off on H3 flight 10 from Tanegashima at 04:41:03 JST on 20 October 2026, which is 19:41:03 UTC on 19 October, and separated into its planned orbit about 71 minutes later. On 21 October JAXA confirmed the spacecraft was healthy and closed its initial critical operations phase, moving on to checks of its onboard equipment. Arrival at Mars is planned for August 2027, with at least 10 g of Phobos due on Earth in July 2031.

name: The derelict fleet in Mars orbit
short_status: Twenty-three objects were in orbit at Mars on 26 August 2026: six working spacecraft, ten dead ones and seven pieces of hardware. Nothing there is tracked, and JPL models only five of the wrecks.

name: What we left behind: parachutes, backshells and heat shields
short_status: Twelve landing sites carry entry hardware identified from orbit, almost all by HiRISE: heat shields, backshells, parachutes, descent stages and Curiosity's tungsten ballast. At the oldest the pieces are only likely.

name: Fobos-Grunt 2, Boomerang and Mars-Grunt
short_status: Paper only, and dormant with no announced end as of 27 August 2026: Boomerang reached technical proposals in 2019 and stopped there for want of money. No hardware was built and no cancellation was ever announced.

name: Mangalyaan-2 (Mars Lander Mission)
short_status: Announced in October 2014 and still unfunded: the Space Commission approved it in February 2025, and the Union Cabinet, which releases the money, had not by 24 August 2026. No Mars window opens in 2030.

name: China's crewed Mars plans
short_status: Stated but not funded. As of 24 August 2026 China has approved no crewed Mars mission; CNSA's roadmap, presented to the UN in January 2024, puts crewed Mars in the 2040 to 2050 band, behind a lunar landing around 2030.

name: Starship and Mars
short_status: SpaceX has never launched anything to Mars. Starship flew thirteen tests without reaching orbit before Flight 14 reached it on 28 September 2026, and as of that date SpaceX's own website offers cargo to the Martian surface no earlier than 2028.

name: National Mars ambitions
operator: MBRSC and the UAE Space Agency; KASA (South Korea); others
short_status: Two national targets with no Mars hardware behind them: the UAE's Mars 2117 settlement programme of 14 February 2017 and South Korea's 2045 robotic landing goal, set 28 November 2022. Both stood on 24 August 2026.

name: Mars Science Helicopter and Chopper
operator: NASA JPL, NASA Ames and AeroVironment
short_status: Concept work with nothing approved to fly: as of 24 August 2026 neither the Mars Science Helicopter of March 2020 nor the SUV-sized Chopper of December 2024 has a mission, though the rotors have been tested past Mach 1.

name: Mars Life Explorer
short_status: Still a concept as of 24 August 2026, with no new start, funding line or launch date. The 2022 decadal survey made this ice-drilling lander NASA's top medium-class Mars mission, to follow sample return's peak spending.

name: SkyFall
short_status: Adopted by NASA on 24 March 2026, cut from AeroVironment's six-helicopter concept to three: released in mid-air with no lander involved. Launch is December 2028 aboard SR-1 Freedom, landing in autumn 2030.

name: The Impulse and Relativity Mars lander
short_status: Dormant rather than cancelled: announced on 19 July 2022 for a launch as soon as late 2024, moved to 2026 in May 2023, and unmentioned by either company since. No hardware, customer or payload has ever been shown.

name: Commercial Mars Payload Services and Mars Future Missions
short_status: Two budget lines with no mission selected: CMPS was created in NASA's fiscal 2026 request at $200 million, Mars Future Missions enacted at $110 million in January 2026. The low-cost solicitation is due October 2026.

name: LightShip, SpotLight and MARCONI
short_status: Not approved: a Phase A/B1 design study running to mid-2027. ESA's exploration programme was undersubscribed at the November 2025 ministerial, and LightShip was not among the missions confirmed there.

name: Mars Telecommunications Network
short_status: Awarded and under protest: on 1 September 2026 NASA picked Blue Origin for a firm fixed-price contract worth up to about $700 million. Rocket Lab filed a protest with the Government Accountability Office on 11 September; the office has 100 days to rule.

name: Aeolus and the Relativity Mars orbiter
short_status: Announced on 17 June 2026 and still undisclosed in almost every detail: NASA supplies the four-instrument Aeolus payload, Relativity pays for and flies the orbiter. Launch is 2028 on Terran R, which has never flown.

name: Mars Sample Return (NASA and ESA)
short_status: Cancelled: Congress declined to fund it in the appropriations bill signed on 23 January 2026, and ESA member states asked for the cancellation of the Earth Return Orbiter in March 2026. No replacement has been started.

name: Sending people to Mars
short_status: An aspiration with no programme behind it: as of 28 September 2026 we could find no funded human Mars programme, approved architecture or committed landing date anywhere. US space policy sets no Mars date, and its dated human exploration goals are all lunar.

name: Space Reactor-1 Freedom
short_status: Announced on 24 March 2026 for a December 2028 launch: it would be the first spacecraft to propel itself beyond Earth orbit on a fission reactor. By August 2026 it had a requirements-level review and no rocket.

name: Rosalind Franklin rover
short_status: Funded and building hardware as of September 2026: NASA approved its supporting project on 16 April 2026 and selected a Falcon Heavy. ESA still says launch in 2028 and landing in 2030, with no exact dates published.

name: Tianwen-3 (天问三号)
short_status: In development, nothing flown yet: on 12 March 2026 chief designer Liu Jizhong said the spacecraft were in prototype build. CNSA still says launch around 2028 and samples on Earth around 2031.
